A common path is to study funeral services, complete an internship, work as a funeral professional or undertaker, manage a funeral home, and eventually operate a funeral-service organization or provide training.
This work suits steady, careful, empathetic people who can carry emotional weight. If helping people leave with dignity is meaningful to you, this can be a stable career.

Morticians, undertakers, and funeral arrangers plan and conduct funerals. They transport, embalm, and restore the deceased, arrange memorial spaces, and communicate with families to ensure dignified farewell ceremonies.

entries: Morticians and undertakers plan and conduct funerals, transporting, embalming, and restoring the deceased, arranging memorial halls, and communicating with families to ensure dignified farewell ceremonies.
Transport and care for the deceased.

paragraphs: Early in the morning, transport the deceased to the funeral home. During the morning, perform embalming and restorative work and apply cosmetics according to the family's wishes. At midday, review the process with the undertaker and finalize wreaths and attendee lists. In the afternoon, arrange the memorial hall and rehearse. On the ceremony day, accompany the family throughout, then complete cremation and documentation afterward.

In short, they help people leave with dignity. Work includes transporting the deceased, embalming and restorative preparation, arranging memorial halls, conducting ceremonies, coordinating with families, and completing subsequent steps. It requires both skilled hands and emotional intelligence.

That is a net increase of about 900 jobs, with roughly 3,200 annual openings. Median annual pay is about $49,800 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace funeral professionals, but it will take over scheduling and paperwork. Online memorials and digital scheduling handle appointments and notifications, shifting funeral professionals from processing formalities toward caring for the deceased, conducting ceremonies, and comforting families. Purely administrative roles face displacement, while people with practical skills and empathy become more valuable.

The greatest occupational risk is not AI but changing demand structures. Simplified options such as cremation and sea burial are increasing, and online memorials are growing, but care of the deceased and in-person support cannot be replaced. Entry thresholds and credential requirements are also rising.

No matter how intelligent systems become, funeral professionals still use skilled hands, a steady voice, and sound judgment to care for the deceased, conduct ceremonies, and accompany families through the final farewell. People cannot be removed entirely from end-of-life service.
In short, the future shortage is not of people who can schedule, but of funeral professionals with practical skills who lead ceremonies and understand empathy.
